title: Put a front door on the latch: hold the night latch's knob turned and slide the snib down
instruction: Put the door on the latch, so that the bolt stays drawn back after you let go.
context: A rim night latch locks itself whenever the door shuts. People put it on the latch when they step out to the bins or carry shopping in, so the door cannot lock them out; a UK locksmith firm's job records say "Keys accidently being left inside the property account for around 33% of lockout situations" (https://www.keytek.co.uk/blog/beyond-the-lost-key-3-surprising-reasons-youll-be-locked-out-this-winter/). What is hard for a robot: the bolt is sprung, so one hand must turn the knob and keep it turned while the other slides a 12 mm button 6 mm. Let go first and the bolt springs out; slide the snib first and the door is deadlocked instead.
setup: Centimetres from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left, heights above the table. One Yale P77 Traditional Nightlatch, 60 mm backset (https://www.yalehome.co.uk/77-traditional-nightlatch-60mm), fitted as made to a 30 x 30 cm section of a 44 mm white-painted door. The section stands upright across the table, held by two steel angle brackets on its far side; its near face is at x 42.5, it runs from y -28 to its latch edge at y 2. The maker's page gives 550 g and 7.5 x 7.5 x 11 cm overall and calls the inside control an "internal knob handle"; case and knob sizes here are from the dimension drawing and photos on a lock shop's listing (https://www.lockshop-warehouse.co.uk/acatalog/yale-77-traditional-style-nightlatch-reversed-outward-opening.html). The latch case (93 x 66 mm, 25 mm deep, grey-green) is on the near face, flush with the latch edge. The knob (an oval 38 x 25 mm, upright, standing 22 mm off the case) has its axis at y -4, 15 cm above the table. The snib (a round button 12 mm across, 6 mm proud) is on the case 36 mm from the knob's axis toward the latch edge, at the upper end of its 6 mm upright slot. The brass bolt (25 mm tall, 16 mm thick) stands 13 mm out of the latch edge. Turning the knob about 70 degrees (its top away from the latch edge) draws the bolt back; let go, both spring back. The snib slides down only with the bolt fully back, where it holds it, or fully out, where it deadlocks it out (the wrong end state). Stand-ins: the door section for a whole door; the outside cylinder is left off (it plays no part from inside).
scoring: Read at the end of the run from one photo of the latch and a ruler at the door's edge. 1.0: for the last 1 s the bolt stands at most 3 mm out of the door's edge (13 mm at the start), the snib's button is at the lower end of its slot (at least 4 mm below the upper end) and both grippers are at least 5 cm from the latch. 0.5: the same bolt and snib, but a gripper is within 5 cm of the latch, or its position is not known. 0: anything else. That covers the untouched latch, the knob turned and let go (the bolt is out again), the knob still held turned with the snib up, and the snib down with the bolt out (deadlocked).
reset_notes: Slide the snib up: the bolt springs out. Check with the ruler that it stands 13 mm out. Under 10 s; nothing is used up.
fidelity: Rigid parts at the sizes on the maker's page and a lock shop's drawing. The inside of the case is an estimate (the latch was not opened): a pin on the knob pushes the bolt's tail, and a stop on the snib drops into one of two notches. All by contact, springs and joint limits. One rule: a light detent seats the snib at the nearer end of its slot. Estimates to check on the real latch: bolt spring 5 to 10 N, detent 1 N, knob stop 72 degrees, snib 6 mm proud, held bolt 1 mm out.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0; scripted demo (a fixed plan for the fixed layout): 1.0 (twice, 412 steps each)
